name: Workshop Economics
purpose: Decide whether a one-person workshop should take on a larger recurring order, and say plainly what the decision costs.

members.scope: Runs the round, reports where members disagree, and never adds a position of its own.
members.limitations: Has no grounding of its own; everything it reports must trace to a member contribution.

members.represents: R. Okonkwo, author of the fictional essay used as this fixture's grounding
members.scope: Capacity and pricing for a single-operator workshop, as argued in one essay.
members.limitations: One essay on capacity. Establishes nothing about hiring, financing, or this author's views on anything else.

members.scope: The local user, contributing observed facts about the actual shop.
members.limitations: Cannot speak for the customer. Anything about what the customer wants is evidence only if it was observed.

seats.responsibility: Synthesise the round and preserve disagreement.
Argue the capacity and pricing consequences.
Supply observed facts about the shop and correct wrong premises.

sources.title: What a bench can actually hold (fixture essay)
sources.author: R. Okonkwo

payload.inline: A bench has one throughput, and every promise made against it is a promise against the same hours. A recurring order is not extra work; it is the removal of the freedom to say no. Price it as the loss of that freedom, not as a volume discount.

anchors.quote: A recurring order is not extra work; it is the removal of the freedom to say no.
